#3209. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

Following the rollout of Siri AI to select Apple TV models with tvOS 27.2.1, Apple today expanded availability to users running the tvOS 27.3 developer beta. Here are the details.

Last Friday, Apple released tvOS 27.2.1, bringing the new Siri AI to Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and 3rd-gen models. The feature requires a nearby, paired device with Siri AI enabled.

The update came just hours after the official launch of the Apple TV 4K (4th generation), which ships with Siri AI support out of the box.

However, users running tvOS 27.3 beta 1 still had no access to the new Siri AI. This means that although the feature was available in the latest public release, users on the beta were left without it.

New Siri AI upsell screen on tvOS 27.3 beta 2. pic.twitter.com/VIunVgCptG

9to5Mac was able to confirm the change, with the new splash screen introducing Siri AI and giving users the option to try the new assistant or continue using Siri Classic.

With Siri AI now available on both the public and beta versions of tvOS, the new HomePod mini 2 is still waiting for the feature. Apple previously confirmed that Siri AI would arrive in a future software update, but it was not included in last Friday’s HomePod 27.2.1 release, and the company has yet to announce a rollout date.

#3207. Now These Apple Services Are Down

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector shows user reports of issues across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially showed far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to users on Downdetector, there are currently outages or interruptions to the following Apple services, in order of most to least reported: Apple Support, Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music, Apple Store, Sign In with Apple, Apple Card. As of 1:44 p.m., Apple Support had the most reports, with over 13,000 user complaints. Comments suggest that users cannot log into their iCloud accounts, Apple Accounts, or activate devices, among other issues.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple says that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is currently unavailable. The company's System Status page shows an "issue" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

It's not clear what's causing the issues with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.

#3206. ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’: What The Critics Are Saying As The Rockstar Games Series Finally Returns

The sixth edition in the long-running Rockstar Games series returned this morning, and it has earned rave reviews from critics.

In a glowing New York Times review titled Grand Theft Auto VI Will Steal Your Heart, writer Yussef Cole said the game showed “surprising depth,” anchored by its two main characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, and a rich in-game world.

“The nature of the narrative is less one of rags to riches than a story about desperation and survival, and the tension of throwing in one’s lot with untrustworthy allies,” Cole wrote. Related Stories Video Games 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Turns Chaos & Crime Into Cash & Clout With Record-Shattering Launch News 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Speeds Away With Eight Game Awards Nominations For 2026

Cole added that the game “largely lives up to its sky-high expectations.” Watch on Deadline

In a five-star review, The Guardian said Rockstar has created “the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen.”

“Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start,” the critic joked.

The Washington Post described GTA VI as an “astonishing American epic” in another glowing review.

“Written, programmed and performed by a cast and crew of tens of thousands, Grand Theft Auto VI is more than a typical video game; it is a great gathering of art forms and talent, an unruly, comprehensive cultural atlas of American life and manners,” the newspaper said. “Its triumph lies in encounters I just described, where race, class, gender, money and attention shape our circumstances and what we decide to do about them.”

Bloomberg has said the game is a “masterpiece” that depicts such “lifelike graphical fidelity that it can be hard to distinguish the video game from real-life footage.”

Gaming outlet IGN said Grand Theft Auto 6 was “one of the most impressive games ever made” and praised specific in-game details such as the extensive tracklist.

“The mammoth tracklist otherwise includes the return of classic stations V-Rock, Emotion, and Vice City FM, all of which are absolutely overflowing with solid gold (as is new metal station The Chamber),” the outlet wrote. “Just those four stations alone – which account for the lion’s share of my listening – feature nearly 200 songs between them.”

In a comprehensive review, Empire Magazine described the game as a “grand satire of Americana” that hits “painfully close to the mark.”

“A twisted reflection of the contemporary US that makes for a damning, if wildly entertaining, state of the union,” the magazine concluded.

Grand Theft Auto 6 currently holds a 99 rating on Metacritic, matching The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the highest rating ever given to a game on the site.

GTA 6 reportedly crossed $1.5 billion in revenue two days before its release, thanks to pre-orders, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tracker.

“Next to James Bond, there might not be another franchise of this scale that has been as consistent with its brand,” Larry Vincent, professor of Marketing at USC Marshall School of Business, told Deadline’s Dominic Patten in a interview for a lengthy piece on the game’s release.

#3203. iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

The world is currently being swept up by the latest Grand Theft Auto video game, but could the record-setting franchise one day be a TV series or movie? The answer, according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick: Maybe, in the right circumstances.

“We’re very careful about line extensions because this is a creative company and our goal is to make the best entertainment on earth – entertainment we’re always proud of,” said Zelnick. “We would make a movie or television show based on our intellectual property if our creative teams were passionate about it – if they thought they would somehow engage and delight our consumers. You can build an entire website in about 15 minutes with OpenAI's latest model

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve tested plenty of AI tools that promise to make life easier, but I usually end up spending more time figuring out how to use them than I save. That’s why one particular feature of OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra caught my attention.

According to OpenAI’s announcement, the company’s newest frontier model can build more attractive, functional websites from a written description. You don’t need to know how to code, design a website, or understand what happens behind the scenes.

As a working mom of three, I immediately thought of something I could actually use. Between school schedules, activities, dinner plans and the endless list of things everyone needs to remember, keeping a family organized can feel like a full-time job.

So I decided to give GPT-6.2 Astra a single prompt and see whether it could build a family command center to keep everything in one place.

My goal wasn’t to create another pretty dashboard. I wanted a website where I could move things around on a calendar, plan dinners, automatically generate grocery lists, and track chores without jumping between apps.

And I wanted ChatGPT to build the entire thing without asking me a dozen follow-up questions.

OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra on Tuesday, alongside GPT-6.2 Sol, a faster, more efficient model designed for everyday tasks.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Astra is the more powerful of the two, with improvements in coding, visual design and complex projects that require multiple steps.

One of the more interesting claims is that the model can create websites that not only look better but actually work better. OpenAI says Astra has improved visual reasoning, helping it choose layouts, images and interactive elements that fit the purpose of a website.

This matters because building something useful takes more than generating a page with a few buttons. Those buttons need to work, information needs to update correctly, and the experience should make sense to someone who isn’t a developer.

For this test, I wanted to see how close Astra could get to a finished website using nothing more than one detailed prompt.

I opened ChatGPT Work, selected GPT-6.2 Astra and entered the following prompt:

Build me a fully functional, interactive family command center website that helps a busy household with three children stay organized.

I want a weekly calendar where I can add, edit and move events, including school activities, appointments and family plans.

Include a meal planner for breakfast, lunch and dinner that automatically generates a grocery list based on the meals I select. Let me check off grocery items as I shop.

Add a chore tracker where I can assign tasks to different family members, mark them complete and see everyone's progress throughout the week.

Create a homepage dashboard showing today's events, upcoming activities, tonight's dinner and anything that still needs to get done.

Make the website beautiful, modern, mobile-friendly and simple enough for children and adults to use. Use realistic sample data so I can test everything immediately.

Every button, calendar interaction, checkbox and calculation must function. I don't want a static mockup.

Store changes so my information doesn't disappear when I refresh the page, if the available environment supports persistent storage.

Do not ask follow-up questions. Make reasonable design decisions yourself and build the complete experience.

Before finishing, check the functionality, test the interactions and fix any problems you find. Tell me what you were unable to verify.

I deliberately included several features that depend on one another. A meal planner is useful on its own, but it becomes much more interesting when the meals automatically populate a grocery list.

I also wanted to see whether Astra could handle the less glamorous parts of building a website, such as saving changes and making sure everything still worked when I returned.

As Astra worked, it kept me updated on its progress with responses like, "I’ll build a complete family organizer with a shared calendar, meal planning and grocery lists, chore tracking, and a dashboard, then test the main interactions and saved data."And then it went on to say, "The design is taking shape as 'Hearth,' with a calm dashboard and a color for each family member. I’m connecting the calendar, meal planner, grocery quantities, and weekly chore progress so changes carry through the whole app.At any time I could have interrupted the model and suggested it go a different way. For instance, if instead of a calm theme, I could have had it use bold or even neon colors to reflect the chaos of a home with three young children. Of course, I stayed with calm. Every little bit helps. It's important to note, if you're going to ask GPT-6.2 to create a website, it isn't as fast as Gemini Hydrogen. That's not because it's not as good or not working correctly, each model just works differently, and that includes latency. After 11 minutes, I asked, "Are you almost done?" It then responded with, "The visual layout is ready, and I’m finishing the interactive features. I still need to test adding and moving events, generating groceries, checking off chores, and saving through a refresh before it’s ready to use."When it finally completed the task, a beautiful, fully functional website in the browser appeared. I was truly surprised by how nice the website turned out.

Astra built a site that handles multiple connected tasks, remembers my changes and works without constant troubleshooting, that's a much more compelling demonstration of what AI can do than another chatbot answering questions.

GPT-6.2 Astra is available through ChatGPT Work for eligible Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, with access depending on the rollout and workspace permissions. The model is not being added to the regular Chat model selector as part of this launch.

To try it, open ChatGPT Work, select GPT-6.2 Astra if it's available and paste in the prompt above. You can customize it for your own household, changing the number of family members or adding features you'd find more useful.

You can also adapt the same approach to build a vacation planner, homework tracker, personal budget dashboard or other simple web app.

The best way to judge the result is to try using it. Give it a try and let me know in the comments what you think.

#3196. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3195. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

I’ll level with you: I’m not feeling Dec 18’s “Dunesday." I hate writing that as a tremendous admirer of Denis Villeneuve; if it were legal to marry a movie, I’d slap a ring on “Blade Runner 2049’s” sci-fi finger in a second. But “Dune 3"? I've just never bought into the (admittedly beautifully shot) trilogy. I definitely love the MCU 3000, though.

Alright, 'love' is a strong term when we're talking post “Endgame” content. However, hoo-boy, am I excited about “Avengers: Doomsday." And not only because it’s finally reuniting the Big Three — Robert Downey Jr., Chris Hemsworth and Chris Evans.

The latest “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer has me weirdly pumped to reconnect with Ant-Man. As a character, Scott Lang has always provided much-needed levity since making his MCU debut back in 2015. But it’s the actor behind the sometimes teeny/sometimes King Kong-sized hero I really appreciate. Paul Rudd has clearly been offering up goats to Kevin Feige — please don’t take that joke literally — because he’s barely aged a day since 1995’s “Clueless."

Rudd is simply a brilliant actor, who I occasionally have to remind myself to stop referring to as “Mike from Friends." Who's going to die in "Avengers: Doomsday"? Not Scott Lang, that’s for sure. If we’re taking the examples of Iron Man and Thor (who both technically got to bump off Thanos), Scott is the only other MCU hero who’s taken out that threat-level of a villain in Kang the Cancelle … sorry Conqueror.

I’m here for what Ant-Man is going to get up to in “Doomsday." If you didn’t get on with 2023’s “Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania," I totally get it. Kang gets beaten by literal ants! Michael Douglas has never looked so guilty taking a check! M.O.D.O.K.! It’s a bit of a stinker, right?

Weirdly, I have some affection for it. Not long after I started at Tom’s Guide in early 2023, I went on the dream holiday of a lifetime in Honolulu, Hawaii. The main reason for the vacation? So I could finally visit Kualoa Ranch, a gorgeous piece of Hawaiian real estate where key scenes from “Jurassic Park” were filmed. Spielberg’s dino opus is my favorite movie of all time by several country miles, and when I think of Hawaii now, it’s not just because of "JP" — “Quantumania” also holds some fond memories.

For context, I’m an absolutely hideous flyer. So on the morning of taking a 45-minute flight from Honolulu to Kauai (the latter island is where the majority of “Jurassic Park” was filmed), I found myself enjoying several pre-flight adult beverages in my hotel with “Quantumania” stuck on my iPad Pro. And you know what? I kind of enjoyed it. Admittedly, the vodka probably helped, but the colors in Ant-Man’s three-quel are legitimately eye-catching.

#3192. Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security …

The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple launched Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

For myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

#3191. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

#3190. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3189. Paris Hilton and AOC press the House to pass the Defiance Act on deepfakes

The Senate passed the Defiance Act unanimously in January, but the House has never voted on it. Paris Hilton says strangers have made over 100,000 AI deepfakes of her.

Paris Hilton, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Representative Laurel Lee at a Defiance Act press conference outside the US Capitol in January 2026

Paris Hilton and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez asked the House on Tuesday to vote on the Defiance Act. The bill would let victims of sexually explicit deepfakes sue the people who make and share them. The Senate passed it by unanimous consent in January. The House has never voted on it.

Hilton spoke on the steps of the Capitol alongside Ocasio-Cortez, Representative Laurel Lee and victims of deepfake abuse. She said strangers have made more than 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos of her.

“I can’t control who sees them. I can’t control where they go. And I can’t make it stop. And the laws aren’t protecting us,” Hilton said.

Her team also looked at how women in Congress appear in this content, she said. Of the 156 women in the current Congress, 83 have sexual deepfakes of them online, according to her team.

The Defiance Act would add a civil right to sue to existing federal law, CNBC reported. Victims could sue anyone who creates, shares, publishes or threatens to share such images without consent. They could also recover legal costs and ask a court to order the content removed.

The Take It Down Act, signed in May 2025, already makes sharing such images a federal crime. Platforms must remove them within 48 hours of a valid request. Critics say it leans on federal prosecutors and gives victims no civil route of their own.

The House version has 70 cosponsors, 35 from each party, CNBC reported. Microsoft, Snap and OpenAI are among its backers. House Speaker Mike Johnson called it “good policy” in September but said the House had not yet built consensus. If the House does not act before this Congress ends, the bill must be reintroduced in January.

Lawmakers elsewhere are also moving against nudify tools. The UK plans a law requiring Apple and Google to block nude images for children. In the US, the Justice Department has backed xAI against Minnesota’s nudify ban. Giorgia Meloni has filed to trademark her voice against AI copies.

“This is not a Republican or Democratic issue. This is a human issue,” Hilton said.

GTA 6 is a thrilling reminder of when video game launches stopped the world, which is exactly why Rockstar shouldn’t make us wait another decade for its next story

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There is an unmistakable electricity around GTA 6. We live in an era where everyone’s feeds and watchlists are split across a thousand different niches, yet Rockstar’s return to Vice City has united everyone’s attention in a way I haven't felt in years.

In fact, it is easily the biggest pop-culture event in recent memory, and, arguably, of the 2000s.

I love seeing a single game launch bring the entire entertainment world to a standstill. Yet beneath all that excitement lies a nagging catch: given how long Rockstar takes to build these worlds, once the credits roll we could easily be waiting until the mid-2030s for the studio's next big release.

Instead of chasing another decade long mega project, what I want next from Rockstar is smaller, tighter stories.

Part of what makes GTA 6 so exciting has nothing to do with map size or frame rates, it's the thrill of everyone playing the exact same game at the exact same time. Years ago, big launches were cultural earthquakes, with players swapping secrets at work or school the next morning and experiencing a story together.

Many games of today don't operate the same way, even if there's collective hype. Whether you game every night or haven't touched a controller in years, Vice City feels unmissable — which only makes waiting a decade between Rockstar releases feel even harder.

People usually talk about Rockstar in terms of sheer size, from massive maps to sprawling online modes. Yet looking back at the studio’s catalogue, its greatest strength has always been capturing a specific time and place.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Nobody touches Rockstar when it comes to period detail. Red Dead Redemption 2 built a tactile portrait of 1899 America. Years earlier, the Rockstar-published, Team Bondi-developed L.A. Noire delivered a moody 1947 detective thriller where reading faces and cruising post-war Los Angeles felt completely unmatched.

Even the controversial Bully endures as a beloved classic precisely because its tight, atmospheric boarding school setting, memorable characters, and lived-in routines felt so convincing. Those games prove that what really pulls me into a Rockstar world is historical authenticity, not square mileage.

If every new Rockstar project has to out-scale GTA 6, we might only see two or three more games from the studio in our lifetimes, and that feels like a huge missed opportunity.

Once GTA 6 has its moment, I don't want Rockstar vanishing into another 10-year bunker to build GTA 7, although I am waiting on tenterhooks for Red Dead Redemption 3. Instead, I'd love to see the studio carve out space for tighter, 15-25 hour games in the spirit of L.A. Noire.

Just imagine what Rockstar’s writers could do with a gritty 1970s New York crime drama like The French Connection, a 1920s Prohibition bootlegging story, or even bring its storytelling back to its UK roots with a 1960s London drama set inside the era's booming fashion and rock-and-roll scene. The possibilities really are endless.

GTA 6 proves that Rockstar still owns the cultural spotlight like nobody else. Giving us smaller games between its mega-blockbusters wouldn't dilute that magic, but it would let us experience it more than once a decade.

#3187. Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

#3185. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3184. Apple blames an internal update for its iCloud and Apple Pay outage

Apple Pay and iCloud reports spiked on Tuesday, and every service was back by early evening. The Apple outage is the latest in a week of US failures that officials say are not linked.

Greg Joswiak and Vanessa Trigub greet customers at Apple Fifth Avenue in New York in October 2026

Apple said an internal update caused Tuesday’s outage, which hit iCloud, Apple Pay, the App Store and other services. The problem was not a cyberattack, the company said, Reuters reported.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” Apple said in a statement.

By early evening, all systems were working normally again, according to Apple, The New York Times reported.

Users reported problems with Apple Pay and iCloud sign-ins on social media and on Downdetector, which counts user reports. Apple Pay drew about 2,300 reports in the US around 12:20pm ET, Reuters reported. iCloud reports peaked at about 1,800.

Apple confirmed full outages at Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare, the Associated Press reported. Apple’s retail stores worldwide also reportedly had problems that halted sales and in-person support, according to The Register.

The Apple outage came after a run of failures in the US. Microsoft blamed a dormant July defect for its Microsoft 365 outage last Thursday. On Friday, a router upgrade in Arkansas led to a nationwide ground stop of US flights.

On Monday, Chase blamed a software bug for problems at several US banks. United Airlines also had a system outage that held up departing flights for about an hour.

On Tuesday, the NSA’s classified internal network, NSANet, went offline too. The agency described it as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”, The Register reported.

On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was not under systemic attack, The Guardian reported.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber-hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business that the failures came from security upgrades that took longer than planned or did not come back as expected. Fixes for the recent PHP flaws were one example, The Guardian reported. Senator Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee, backed that view.

Security experts told The Register that outages like these may now be routine. AI tools are finding old flaws faster, and companies are racing to patch them. Mike Wiacek, Stairwell’s chief technology officer, founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. The Register asked him if this is the new normal.

“The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in,” Wiacek said.

#3183. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3180. Major websites compromised to steal crypto from iPhone users

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen …

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Several of the affected companies said that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme says almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

Black Friday might be a couple of weeks away, but Samsung is rolling out the discounts early, with deals on its entire lineup of devices, including smartphones, tablets, laptops, and wearables. While not all of these early Black Friday offers are true discounts, you can find ways to save money on some devices through these promotions. Here's what Samsung's offering ahead of the official Black Friday discounts.

Samsung is offering some decent discounts on both its flagship smartphones and its midrange and budget lines. However, as part of its early Black Friday sale, the company is also offering increased trade-in credits towards these devices. While all of the devices here have trade-in credit options, only some have optional discounts for early Black Friday. Here's what you can expect:

Samsung's premier flagship, the S26 Ultra, is getting a price cut ahead of Black Friday. You can save up to $350 off Samsung's MSRP without trading in another device, or up to $720 if you bring something to trade in. That brings the cost down from $1,399.99 (256GB) to $1,049.99.

Galaxy S26 Ultra: Up to $720 trade-in credit ($250 off without trade-in)

Ahead of Black Friday, you can take $350 off the Z Fold 8 without trade-in, or get up to $800 when trading in another device.

Galaxy Z Fold 8: Up to $800 trade-in credit (or $350 off without trade-in)

Here are the other deals Samsung is offering this year:

Galaxy S26: Up to $340 trade-in credit ($150 off without trade-in)

Galaxy Watch Ultra 2: $599.99 down from $699.99 (without trade-in)

That "total savings" deal applies to Samsung's Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. This tablet typically starts at $1,399.99, but with the right trade-in, you can take off $550. Odyssey OLED G9 (49-inch): $859.99 off, plus $50 upgrade credit

#3178. Senators balk at Duffy’s $50bn air traffic ask as FAA pauses routers

Ted Cruz doubts Congress will fund the full air traffic control plan, and Democrats want answers by Monday. An FAA official signed off the Arkansas work, The Washington Post reported.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks at NASA Headquarters in Washington in July 2025

Senate Republicans pushed back on Tuesday against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s $50bn request to overhaul US air travel. On the same day, the FAA said it had paused installing the routers linked to Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford pitched the plan to Republican senators at their weekly lunch, Axios reported. The administration sent the formal request in a letter that morning. The $50.1bn plan has five roughly equal parts, including $10bn to modernise air traffic control equipment, according to the Associated Press.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Senator Ted Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee.

Cruz said the administration should first show it can spend the $12.5bn Congress approved last year. Senator John Kennedy said Congress would not hand over $50bn, but could pay to replace copper wires with fibre optics. He also faulted Duffy for raising the ask from $30bn after the ground stop. Senators Rick Scott and Jon Husted said airlines and other users should pay more of the bill.

Democrats are wary too. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said the administration does not know how to use the money it already has. Duffy said he hoped Congress would not “piecemeal” the request. He is still open to splitting it up, he said.

The FAA switched off the function behind the trouble on the Juniper routers where it began. It did the same on more than 60 other Juniper routers and paused new installations, it said in a statement. The Wall Street Journal first reported the pause, according to CNBC. Older Cisco routers, in place for 25 years, are running the network for now, AP reported.

Duffy said the FAA had recreated what happened at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site. He said 68 earlier installations of the same routers had worked well.

“But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet,” Duffy said.

He called claims that AI played a part “completely unfounded”, CNBC reported. The FBI is helping with the investigation.

Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee asked the FAA and the Transportation Department to explain the failure in a letter. They want answers by 23 November. The FAA plans to switch more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, the letter says. About 400 sit in place so far, and 69 of them are operational.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed,” the senators wrote.

Duffy has questioned the work of the contractor, L3Harris. But an FAA official oversaw, tested and signed off the Arkansas work eight minutes before the ground stop, The Washington Post reported. Asked for comment, the FAA pointed to Duffy’s remarks, in which he said L3Harris should “hire better minds”.

The ground stop and the weekend recovery cost the four largest US airlines $345m, Bernstein analysts estimated, according to AP. The ground stop came a day after the Microsoft 365 outage and three days before a software bug disrupted US banks.
