#3177. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

Now that I’ve seen the Slate Truck in person and been inside the $25,000 electric pickup truck, I’m itching to take it out on the road for a proper test drive. In order for Slate to hit that price point, the company stripped the cabin back to the basics — with practically everything being a manual affair. That means crank windows and manual seats, just to name a couple.

Even more surprising is the clutter-free dashboard, which ditches the massive center infotainment touchscreens I often see in the best electric cars and opts for a simple built-in phone mount. While I appreciate the distraction-free philosophy, going without a proper display for navigation is a tough adjustment for daily driving. That’s exactly where the CarpodGo T4 Plus — which offers seamless CarPlay and Android Auto support — comes in to save the day.

Honestly, if you intend to buy the Slate Truck, it’s easily the first upgrade I’d recommend getting. Here’s why.

The CarpodGo T4 Plus adds a 10.9-inch, 1,000-nit touchscreen to any vehicle with zero permanent wiring, giving you smooth 60fps wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto in minutes. Its magnetic quick-release base lets you snap the display off when you park without unplugging cables, while Display Only Bluetooth Mode routes audio straight to your speakers. Don't forget to click the coupon to drop the price down to $229. If you're looking for something smaller, there's also the CarpodGo T4 with an 8.9-inch touchscreen.

One of the biggest reasons why I recommend the CarpodGo T4 Plus is that installing it is a breeze. In fact, I’d say it’s just as easy as setting up a dashcam — only much quicker. And the best part? It requires zero permanent dashboard modifications or wiring.

While the Slate Truck appears to tuck its 12V DC outlet inside the frunk rather than the cabin, I was able to power the display directly via USB-C in a Mazda CX-30, making it an easy plug-and-play fit for the Slate Truck's interior USB ports. The setup required me to attach the included fixed console mount onto a flat surface on the dash, plug in the power cable, and snap the screen onto the magnetic quick-release base.

Since the power runs straight through the base's pogo-pin connection, I’m able to lift the 10.9-inch screen right off whenever I park without fumbling with dangling cords. In my opinion, its plug-and-play experience perfectly suits the Slate Truck and its minimalist dashboard above.

Once powered on, the 10.9-inch, fully laminated IPS touchscreen gives me plenty of room for split-screen navigation and media controls — something I wouldn’t get from a phone clipped to the dash.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Having wireless access to both Apple CarPlay and Android Auto makes the CarpodGo T4 Plus the ultimate solution for the Slate Truck's barren cabin. Instead of juggling a phone mount for turn-by-turn directions, you get the familiar, driver-friendly interface of Google Maps (complete with the new Immersive Navigation experience), Apple Maps, Spotify, and hands-free messaging right on a wide touchscreen — running at a smooth 60 fps, so swiping and zooming feel genuinely responsive.

Even better is how flexible it is when it comes to handling audio, especially since the Slate Truck doesn’t come with any factory-installed speakers. Out of the box, the CarpodGo T4 Plus can output audio directly through its own built-in speaker, which works great for quick navigation prompts and podcasts — but it lacks the depth needed for listening to music.

If you want fuller sound for music on longer drives, though, I recommend leaning on its Display Only Bluetooth Mode, which lets the screen handle all the CarPlay or Android Auto visuals while your phone routes audio straight to an external Bluetooth speaker.

What makes CarpodGo's lineup such a practical solution for Slate Truck buyers is that you aren't locked into a one-size-fits-all screen. Depending on how much dashboard real estate you want to give up — and how much you want to spend — you can choose between the CarpodGo T4 Plus, the standard CarpodGo T4, or the CarpodGo Mini.

While all three deliver the same 1,000-nit brightness, 60fps wireless CarPlay and Android Auto responsiveness, and magnetic quick-release convenience, they differ mainly in size and price. For example, the CarpodGo T4 offers everything the T4 Plus does, but in a smaller 8.9-inch footprint that won’t crowd the dashboard as much. Meanwhile, I’ve set up the CarpodGo Mini as well and love its smaller 6.9-inch screen, which features a MagSafe-style magnetic mount.

Sure, these are all great options for early adopters of the Slate Truck, but they have practical applications in other vehicles, too. Whether you're trying to modernize an older car that never came with a touchscreen or you bought a newer vehicle that lacks native CarPlay or Android Auto support, CarpodGo offers one of the cleanest, most versatile ways to bring smart connectivity to virtually any cabin.

The CarpodGo Mini features a 6.9-inch, 1,000-nit screen that delivers 60fps wireless CarPlay and Android Auto. What makes it slightly different apart from its size is how it packs a MagSafe-style magnetic mount, easily letting you snap the screen off when you park. And with Dual-Bluetooth Pure Display Mode, it sends audio straight to your car's speakers so sound quality doesn't drop.

#3174. Nebius CTO Danila Shtan says ideas matter again now that execution is cheap

Danila Shtan told the TNW Podcast that AI coding agents have him building prototypes again. The Nebius CTO also says the sovereignty debate is sometimes over-hyped.

TNW’s Cristian Dina (left) and Nebius CTO Danila Shtan at HumanX in Amsterdam, 24 September 2026

Asked what breaks first when a company grows as fast as Nebius, Danila Shtan gave a one-word answer: everything. The scale and the pace of growth test everything his team builds, all the time, the Nebius CTO told TNW.

“You start building, you have some expectations about the growth or the client’s needs or the performance they need, and they come to surprise you every day.” Danila Shtan, CTO of Nebius

Shtan described Nebius as a Dutch company and one of the largest AI clouds in the world. He spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at HumanX in Amsterdam on 24 September. That day he also joined a fireside chat on the main stage about making AI agents work at scale.

Earlier episodes featured Alexander Rinke of Celonis, Kristin Fracchia of Gamma, and Daniel Dines of UiPath. The full conversation is in the video below.

Nebius provides the infrastructure for training and running AI models and for building applications on them, Shtan said. He leads software development, so his team builds the software that runs on the servers.

“They need access to high performance computing, which is essentially the heart and the blood and everything of the current AI revolution, hype, whatever you call it.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Some customers spend hundreds of millions on the platform, he said. Others spend $50 to run a small slice of compute for half an hour of internal experiments.

Shtan’s team is about 500 to 550 people. His day is mostly talking to them, he said. He checks on projects and gives feedback when something goes very wrong. Nebius builds a platform, but it also builds data centres, which he called a parallel organisation.

AI coding agents have him building again. He can test an idea in hours or days and show the team a rough prototype instead of talking them through it. His thought process was always faster than his implementation skills, he said, and agents now take on that part.

A significant portion of Nebius’s customers are American companies, Shtan said. American customers use European capacity, and European customers use American capacity.

European governments talk about sovereignty as infrastructure, he said. The US government talks about models and capabilities. Large companies talk about not depending on a single model vendor. He called all of these angles correct.

“I feel like sometimes they’re over-hyped, and this is not good for anyone. It’s not good for business.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Nebius wants to be one of the most important independent AI cloud companies in the world, Shtan said. Much of today’s AI capacity sits with vertical players that own the chips, the data centres, the models and the apps. He wants alternatives at every layer, including model vendors and consumer apps.

“So we are all for diversity, and we are all for, like, building this independent layer of AI because too much power in one company’s hands, even if it’s a good company is never a good idea.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Its biggest challenge is growth, he said. Demand keeps rising for large, small and specialised models, and the bottleneck is no longer only GPUs. It is also memory, disks, servers, electricity, land and high-voltage equipment.

Shtan has been an engineering manager for about 25 years. He started as a software developer and moved quickly into managing people. He has worked in warehouse automation, retail, fintech, biotech, a news outlet and a classifieds website. Later he moved into developer tooling, clouds and Nebius.

For young builders, he said, this is a great time, because a large team is no longer needed to ship a successful product. Taste in product and the ability to sell it now matter more. Five years ago, he said, the maxim was that ideas don’t matter and execution does.

“Now, execution is quite cheap, so ideas matter again.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Companies fail at AI when they treat it as magic, he said. His advice is to learn its limits, experiment, fail and try again.

“AI is not a magical thing. It’s a tool.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

#3172. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

It’s almost time to return to Panem as the next chapter of “The Hunger Games,” “Sunrise on the Reaping,” arrives in theaters on Friday (Nov. 20). It’ll tell the story of the 50th annual Hunger Games, known as the Quarter Quell, when a certain Haymitch Abernathy stepped into the arena. As a “Hunger Games” superfan, I can’t wait to watch it. Yes, my tickets are booked!

If you’re also feeling the hype, you might be looking for a few dystopian movies to keep you fed until “Sunrise on the Reaping." And that’s why I’ve rounded up a trio of worthwhile picks to keep you entertained until you can head to your nearest multiplex. There’s a Japanese thriller that also focuses on a teen deathmatch, a YA adaptation that is actually good (a real rarity), and a Spielberg movie that’s a pop culture-stuffed high-tech adventure.

These dystopian movies will keep your “Hunger Games” hype high until you can watch “Sunrise on the Reaping” in cinemas later this week.

You can’t discuss “The Hunger Games” franchise without somebody popping up to declare “it’s just a ‘Battle Royale’ rip-off.” While I think that argument is pretty asinine, I definitely agree that any fans of “Hunger Games” should check out this 2000 Japanese dystopian action-thriller. It also centers on a group of teens forced to fight to the death, but the Panem pageantry is stripped away. This deathmatch is even more visceral and significantly more violent — “Battle Royale” got an R-rating for very good reason.

Set in a Japan besieged by juvenile delinquency, the government institutes a yearly event called Battle Royale, in which a random high school class is taken to a remote island, each is given a duffle bag containing an assortment of supplies and a random weapon, and then they have three days to kill or be killed. Without the sci-fi trappings of “The Hunger Games,” “Battle Royale” focuses squarely on the horrors of children being forced to fight to the death.

In the wake of “The Hunger Games’” success (and “Twilight” before it), Hollywood studios scrambled to adapt any YA novel they could get their hands on. This led to awful films like “Beautiful Creatures,” “The Giver,” and “The Mortal Instruments” (to name just a few). Most didn’t even get one sequel, let alone adapt the whole series, but a rare success story was “The Maze Runner,” which actually completed its franchise run, with a full trilogy.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Based on the novels by James Dashner, “The Maze Runner” movie took the right lessons from “Hunger Games” with a solid young cast, headlined by Dylan O’Brien, and smart direction. It follows a teenage boy named Thomas (O’Brien) who awakens in a vast clearing surrounded by a gigantic stone maze. Along with his fellow teens trapped in the mysterious place, he has to solve the maze to earn his freedom and learn why he was placed there.

The sequels, “The Scorch Trials” and “The Death Cure,” are also pretty good. Though book purists will be disappointed to learn they substantially differ from the novels, stripping away the narrative twists of Dashner’s written work in favor of a more streamlined Hollywood approach.

Watch "The Maze Runner" on Prime Video (buy/rent) now

Dystopian movies don’t have to be excessively dour. Case in point, Steven Spielberg’s “Ready Player One,” which is full of color, larger-than-life set pieces and endless references to decades gone by, especially the 1980s. In fact, there are probably too many pop culture references, though in fairness to Spielberg, that is also a common criticism of the Ernest Cline novel on which the movie is based. Despite its flaws — it’s a theme park movie, fun in the moment, but also artificial — “Ready Player One” is a breezy watch, and a big midpoint sequence pays homage to one of the best Kubrick flicks ever.

Set in 2045, it’s a grim time for humanity. The population escapes the bleakness of the real world via the Oasis, a virtual reality construct where people can be anything they want. When the Oasis’ creator, James Halliday (Mark Rylance), dies, a posthumous recording kickstarts a hunt through the virtual world for three Easter Eggs; whoever finds the final one will be granted control of the digital universe. Our hero is Wade Watts (Tye Sheridan), who is hoping to find the prize before a sinister corporation.

Rory is a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom’s Guide based in the UK. He covers a wide range of topics but with a particular focus on gaming and streaming. When he’s not reviewing the latest games, searching for hidden gems on Netflix, or writing hot takes on new gaming hardware, TV shows and movies, he can be found attending music festivals and getting far too emotionally invested in his favorite football team.

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3169. How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

#3168. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

For AI features that depend on server-based models, each device running iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, or macOS 27.3 will have limited daily access to advanced AI features. These include complex Siri AI requests, Image Playground, certain Photos app editing tools, and more.

The only iCloud+ tier that doesn’t include higher limits is the $0.99/month plan.

Read more: Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

In the Shortcuts app, the ‘Use Model’ action lets you choose between a few different model options, including Cloud, Cloud Pro, On-Device, and ChatGPT.

New perks? SiriAi was introduced without any identified user costs at all, that's the reference point.

So - what is the per device daily usage limit? It appears to be undefined, hence offering 2x, 5x, 10x, or 20x of this undefined value seems like a confusing value proposition.

The linked article mentions that the undefined usage limit is per device, but that the iCloud usage increases are per account. So this 'perk' is an increase over a single device usage limit or the aggregated limits of all your applicable devices?

I suppose the cost of buying increased SiriAi usage directly is still undefined as well? If the author has additional information on these questions, that would be appreciated.

Similar to Apple’s other AI usage limits, your access to the Cloud Pro model in Shortcuts increases if you have a higher storage plan. Per this support document, the 200GB plan supports standard limits, the 2TB plan offers 5x access, followed by 10x on the 6TB plan and 20x on the 12TB plan.

iCloud+ already provided far more than just increased cloud storage, but with iOS 27.3 it’s set to be an asset for AI power users too.

#3166. Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in casting Pattinson as Bond

Jeff Bezos also told Nvidia’s board not to hire an outsider to replace Jensen Huang. His AI start-up Prometheus has raised $14.5bn, and Blue Origin is testing its tools.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos at Blue Origin in Cape Canaveral, Florida, in February 2026

Jeff Bezos said on Tuesday he was “heavily involved” in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. He told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman that five finalists did full screen tests. Once the team watched them, the choice was clear.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob,” Bezos said.

Bezos spoke at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference. Vik Bajaj, his co-founder at the AI start-up Prometheus, joined him on stage. He also gave the Nvidia board advice on replacing Jensen Huang and shared new figures on Prometheus.

Amazon MGM Studios named Pattinson as the new Bond on Monday. Amazon bought MGM in 2022, and this is the first Bond casting under its control.

The team cut a large shortlist down to five finalists, Bezos said. Each did “real old-fashioned screen tests” of three scenes, in full costume, on real sets and with other actors. The group, director Denis Villeneuve among them, spent a couple of hours on Friday reviewing the tests. They made the final call that day.

At first the team leaned slightly against Pattinson because of his fame, Bezos said. They weighed picking someone less famous.

“But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond,” Bezos said.

Asked if Huang should return to Nvidia, Bezos said he did not know what happened in the board meetings. Huang said on Tuesday he would come back if asked. The board has ruled out his return.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said.

Outside CEOs in complex companies have a “vanishingly small chance of succeeding”, he added. Hiring one should be a last resort. Amazon’s own handover is no guide, he said, because it followed a plan that ran for years. Huang, he said, deserves admiration and respect “no matter what”.

Bezos said his AI start-up Prometheus has about 250 staff and has raised roughly $14.5bn. Prometheus has already put much of that into computing power. The company builds AI models for engineering and manufacturing, which he called “AI for atoms”.

Its tools have designed analogue chips and radios in 12 hours, he said. That work would take a team of 10 to 20 people six to nine months. Blue Origin, his space company, is testing the tools on two projects in a private trial with early customers. He gave no date for a public launch.

Elon Musk is merging his companies. Asked if he would do the same with Prometheus, Blue Origin and Amazon, Bezos called it a funny idea. He said he had “nothing to announce”.

He also defended his contacts with President Donald Trump, who he said “reaches out a lot”. Shutting business leaders out is a mistake, he said. Politicians who blame Big Tech for high living costs are picking a villain, he added. They should fix the root cause instead.

#3162. Trump administration says the wave of US tech outages is not connected

A senior official said there is no sign of a cyberattack behind failures at the FAA, Microsoft and the NSA.

President Donald Trump on the South Lawn of the White House on October 5, 2026.

A senior Trump official said on Wednesday there is no sign that a cyberattack caused the recent run of US tech outages. Nor is there any sign the outages were planned together, CNBC reported.

They include last Friday’s nationwide flight halt by the US aviation agency, the FAA, and a long Microsoft Outlook outage. The NSA’s secret network also went down.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said there was no proof linking the outages or pointing to hostile groups, Fox News reported.

President Donald Trump played down the disruptions on Tuesday, during a trip to the Philippines.

“We are not under systemic attack,” Trump told reporters in Manila, according to Reuters.

Tech problems have hit every weekday since last Thursday, when a Microsoft outage took down email for many companies, Reuters reported. JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug for its problems on Monday. On Tuesday, Apple said an internal update had caused outages across its services.

The NSA said its network was briefly degraded during routine maintenance, but that its most important functions kept working.

The FAA has not yet published the cause of the router failure behind the ground stop. Congress had warned that the agency’s rushed upgrade could lead to outages, CP24 reported.

Some lawmakers, including Trump allies, have asked for briefings on the outages.

The iPhone Duo comes with a few trade-offs you shouldn't have to accept on a $2,000 phone; one of which is the lack of Face ID. We know Apple's engineers are prioritising it for the inevitable iPhone Duo 2, but while we wait, an iOS 27 update could bridge the gap.

The iOS 27.3 beta introduces a new facial unlock option for iPhone Duo owners using the device's front-facing camera. It's a bit like Face ID Lite: users will need to authenticate with Touch ID every 45 minutes to use it, and they'll still need to resort to Touch ID for certain actions, like authorizing Apple Pay or filling in logins from Passwords.

Duo users will only be able to use the Unlock with Front Camera feature on the external 5.4-inch display. So, if the phone is unfolded, you can't use the under-display camera on the inner screen to achieve the same result.

Unlock with Front Camera can be found in the Touch ID & Passcode menu in your settings. However, you'll need to have an Apple Developer account and be running the iOS 27.3 developer beta before you can enable it.

If you want to try it for yourself, remember to be careful when installing beta software and ideally create a backup of your iPhone first. Once you're running the beta, switching the feature on is a simple toggle.

Go to your Settings app and scroll down to TouchID & Passcode. Tap the option and enter your passcode to proceed.

You'll see the option to toggle on Unlock with Front Camera. Tap it.

Similar to when you set up Face ID, you'll need to let the iPhone Duo scan your face to activate the feature. Once you've rotated your face, and looked at the camera, you're good to go.

As a leftie, I've been bugged by the fact that I can't use Face ID on the Duo over the last couple of weeks. This new feature could alleviate a huge amount of that frustration.

After trying it myself, it's worked well but I won't go into details at this stage, because it's still early days. Unlock with Front Camera hasn't yet made it to the iOS 27.3 public beta.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

That being said, for those times when you're juggling the Duo one-handed, I can see this addition being a huge bonus. There will, of course, be some limitations, since the Duo's front camera isn't a full TrueDepth camera system. That means you won't be able to unlock it in full darkness and it's less secure — potentially leaving it open to being spoofed by a similar-looking face.

I can also forsee the 45-minute timeout tripping folks up a time or two, though. For most of my workday, the Duo rests either face up or in Tent Mode, and it's easy for 45 minutes to go by without checking — especially if you have one of the best Apple Watches serving you notifications.

We'll dig into how this works over the long term when it becomes a fully public feature but, in the meantime, if there are other potential Duo features you'd like to see added to iOS, let me know about them in the comments.

#3160. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

Making a cafe-quality coffee at home requires at least two of these three things: a great machine, high-quality coffee beans, and someone who knows what they're doing. A well-trained barista can make pro-level coffee on a mid-level machine, as long as they use great beans. An untrained barista will get a top-notch brew with a premium machine and high-quality beans. A trained barista doesn't require expensive beans to make a perfect coffee, as long as they have a good machine.

See what I mean? So what happens if you have a fancy espresso machine and no barista experience? You need to learn how to use it — which a lot of us simply don't have time for. Why learn how to make good coffee at home when you can get fantastic coffee at the cafe down the street?

Don't fret, though. I just got an exclusive first look at Breville's (Sage) brand-new espresso machine, the Barista Express Neo, and I think it's about to change the coffee game due to one unprecedented, patented feature.

Although only available in the U.K. upon initial release, the Breville/Sage Barista Express Neo is one of the coffee scene's most exciting new arrivals. With the patented SmoothSip technology, say goodbye to dialing in and wasting espresso shots.

Breville/Sage have slapped a very Breville/Sage-coded name onto this feature: SmoothSip(TM). It's in the same vein as Ninja's "NeverClog" blender: a little wacky, although overwhelmingly "We're a corporation, but we're relatable, right, kids?"

SageSpeak nomenclature aside, SmoothSip is genuinely innovative. In short, it's a game changer.

So what does SmoothSip actually do? During extraction, SmoothSip live-adjusts bar pressure to ensure every espresso shot pulls — regardless of a too-fine or too-coarse grind size. How many shots have you wasted due to an incorrect grind size? Mine's definitely in the hundreds.

In theory, if you grind your coffee on step 20 — Breville's default — it will be too coarse, unless you're using really oily, dark beans. But with SmoothSip, the machine will slow down the pump (and, yes, lower that pressure below 9 bars) to extract a 1:2 ratio espresso within 26 seconds.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Think of it like a car engine. If you need to drive 1 mile in 2 minutes, you should drive at 30MPH, right? That will necessitate a steady press on the gas pedal. But what if your car is going at 40MPH? You'll need to apply the brake to slow back down to 30.

That's exactly what SmoothSip is doing — it's slowing down the machine (or speeding it up, if your grind is too fine) to reach that destination in the allotted time.

In short: yes. Yes, espresso is "supposed" to extract at 9 bars of pressure. Obviously, reducing the pressure from 9 bars to 3 bars or up to 15 bars isn't ideal in the grand scheme of coffee nerdiness.

However, after each assisted shot, the machine tells you which grind size you should adjust to. And, at the end of the day, you still get your espresso. Even though it's not "perfect", I would rather drink a slightly "imperfect" espresso shot over a nonexistent espresso shot.

I made an overextracted espresso shot on the original Breville Barista Express and the new Barista Express Neo. While they were both too sour, the Neo shot had a much richer mouthfeel and a better depth of flavor. It was tangibly more drinkable than the Barista Express shot.

The Barista Express Neo isn't just a one-trick pony — even though the SmoothSip trick is pretty neat.

The Neo also has an Acaia scale built in, so it always grinds between 17.6-18g of coffee. Yes, Acaia, as in Pearl S and Lunar fame — but this time you're not paying $200+ for the privilege of weighing out your coffee.

There's also a Baratza grinder built in, which cost between $199 (Baratza Encore ESP) and $899 (Baratza Forte BG). If we go off previous Breville models, the Neo will have a version of the $200 Encore ESP grinder.

As with all Breville machines, the Neo has a PID controller to adjust water temperature throughout the brewing process.

Of course, there's a powerful steam wand — but I noticed it took a while to heat up. Perhaps this was just a demo-sample issue. I'll get to the bottom of it when I review the Barista Express Neo myself.

As you might be able to discern from the £ sign above, the Breville/Sage Barista Express Neo is only available in the U.K. right now. It will come to the U.S., but there's no set calendar date. I believe it will be some time later in 2026, but without a concrete date, I'm reticent to speculate.

Unfortunately, across-the-pond-ers will need to wait for the Neo to make it to their esteemed continent. I'm not sure when that will be, but in the meantime, I'm going to be drinking enough Neo coffee to give me the shakes.

Vanda Research expects about $250m of net retail buying when Anthropic starts trading on Nasdaq on Thursday.

Anthropic expects to price its IPO on Wednesday evening and start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. It is offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each, according to CNBC’s IPO guide.

The Nothing Headphone (a) is down to a record-low $109 from $199, making it a solid option for everyday listening, especially for Android users who can take advantage of LDAC for higher-quality wireless audio. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

The JBL Live 780NC are down to $129.95 from $249.95, making them considerably more appealing than at their original price. Battery life is a major advantage here, with JBL estimating up to 50 hours with noise cancellation enabled and 80 hours without, so frequent charging shouldn't be a concern. They also support LDAC for higher-quality Bluetooth audio with compatible devices. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

Apple’s AirPods Max 2 are down to $449 from $549, saving you $100 on the second-generation over-ears that Apple released earlier this year. While the design hasn’t changed much from the original, the upgrade to Apple’s H2 chip brings improved noise cancellation, while its sound remains among the best you'll find in wireless headphones. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

Soundcore's Q20i headphones are down to $42.69 from $69.99, making them one of the more affordable options for anyone looking for noise-canceling over-ears from a recognizable brand. They're particularly worth considering for students, occasional travelers, or anyone who wants a budget-friendly backup pair.

The Beats Solo 4 are down to $129.95 from $199.95, saving you $70. While these lightweight on-ear headphones don't have active noise cancellation, they offer plenty of flexibility for everyday listening, whether you're using an iPhone or an Android phone, with quick pairing on both platforms, notes this PCMag review.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones have the largest dollar discount in this roundup, dropping $160 from $359 to $199.

That depends on how much you want to spend and where you'll use them. The Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) are worth considering for frequent travelers who prioritize noise cancellation, while the regular Bose QuietComfort Headphones at $199 offer a more affordable premium option. The JBL Live 780NC at $129 are appealing for their long battery life and extensive audio customization, and the Soundcore Q20i at $42.69 make sense if you're shopping on a tighter budget. For Apple users who value ecosystem integration, the AirPods Max 2 are worth considering.

#3154. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.
