#3113. Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Gadgets > VR/AR Productivity

The most fascinating and frustrating device I've used in a long time pushes at the edges of where headsets are heading, and glasses are evolving.

Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

There are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a new class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

Emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

The Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

What’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

Android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

The Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D.

The Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing.

The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

The display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

They have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a big movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view).

When running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

The display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

Other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

The whole Aura interface feels new-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

There’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

It’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides.

There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

That’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted.

The puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

Demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely.

YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

Mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

The refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I said before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

Think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or launches live Gemini when held.

There’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

The display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

Sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

Getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

But what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask.

To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

Connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

Right now, I’m connecting the new iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

Whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort.

The glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

It’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

This is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured.

That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

Xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

But the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually?

Right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close.

The Xreal Aura tested even my new-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

#3112. Lost or stolen Windows laptop? IT can lock it down without wiping it now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The Intune-enabled feature will allow admins to remotely lock down any compromised Windows device.

Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

The new remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the new feature allows IT admins to respond quickly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up

The remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Setting up the remote lock is a straightforward process: Log into the Intune management center, then go to Devices > Windows > Configuration > Create > New Policy > Windows 10 and later > Templates > Custom. This lets admins create a profile for each network-connected device and a device group reserved for lockdown. Locking down a device is as simple as adding it to the group. To unlock, create a second profile and device group, and move the locked device to the new unlock category.

#3111. Apple announces App Store price changes in multiple countries, new California tax rules

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”

#3109. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3108. If You Have $1,000 to Invest in December, These 3 Stocks Are Built to Last a Decade

Microsoft, ASML, and TSMC each pair a competitive advantage with AI-driven demand. Here's what gives each its staying power, and the risks to watch.

By Rick Orford – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›

Microsoft (MSFT -0.55%), ASML (ASML +0.64%), and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +0.76%) (TSMC) are three names worth a closer look for investors looking to hold stocks for the next decade. Each has a powerful competitive edge and exposure to some of the biggest technology trends shaping the future, and all three reported strong quarterly results.

Starting with Microsoft, here's what gives each business its staying power.

Microsoft has spent decades building an ecosystem that businesses and consumers rely on every day, giving it a competitive advantage that goes beyond any single product. And these days, that business model continues to drive growth.

For example, in its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results, Microsoft reported 19% year-over-year revenue growth, with Microsoft Cloud revenue climbing 30% and Azure revenue growing 48%.

Plus, Microsoft is integrating artificial intelligence (AI) across its product portfolio through Copilot, while Azure provides the cloud infrastructure businesses need to develop and run AI applications. As a result, rather than relying on a single AI product, Microsoft has several ways to monetize the technology.

However, the risk is that Microsoft continues to spend heavily on AI infrastructure, and investors still want to see it drive revenue growth.

Still, the majority of Wall Street analysts rate the stock a buy, with an average target price of $636. That implies a potential upside of about 21%. On top of that, at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 26, Microsoft doesn't look particularly expensive given its growth opportunities in cloud computing and AI.

Another company, meanwhile, is supplying something just as important: machines that enable advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

ASML's place in the AI supply chain is extremely hard to replicate. Specifically, the company makes advanced lithography equipment used by manufacturers to produce complex chips that power AI and high-performance computing.

Competing with ASML would require decades of research, engineering expertise, and an extensive global supplier network. As a result, that creates a powerful long-term advantage, especially as AI accelerates demand for advanced chips.

The results are showing up in the numbers.

ASML recently reported record third-quarter net sales of €11.7 billion, as customer demand continued to strengthen amid growing AI spending. In fact, management indicated that customers were already expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030.

But the risk now is ASML's exposure to cyclical spending, export restrictions, and geopolitical tensions.

Still, the vast majority of Wall Street analysts covering the stock rate it a buy or strong buy, with an average target price of $2,112, representing approximately 50% potential upside. Plus, the valuation looks reasonable, with the stock trading at a forward P/E of 23 times.

Meanwhile, another company manufactures many of the world's most advanced chips used in the AI build-out.

TSMC runs the world's leading dedicated semiconductor foundry business, manufacturing chips for some of the world's biggest tech companies.

In turn, this business model allows TSMC to benefit from demand across the semiconductor industry. That means it doesn't need to predict which chip designer will win the AI race.

Instead, it can capture growth across the whole industry. Here's how that has shown up in the numbers.

In its third-quarter 2026 results, TSMC reported revenue growth of around 51% year over year, with its advanced manufacturing technologies making up 79% of total wafer revenue. Looking ahead, management pointed to strong demand for leading-edge manufacturing, including the ramp-up of its two-nanometer technology.

But TSMC's biggest risk is its heavy exposure to tensions between China and Taiwan, as well as U.S.-China trade restrictions.

Despite that, 20 of the 21 Wall Street analysts covering the stock rate it a buy or strong buy, with an average target price of about $587, suggesting 57% potential upside. On top of that, it trades at just 18 times forward P/E, making it relatively attractive to investors bullish on its dominant position in advanced chipmaking.

Together, Microsoft, ASML, and TSMC offer exposure to three of the most important parts of the tech industry, making them excellent picks for the next decade.

Ultimately, Microsoft is the safest option because its ecosystem extends beyond any single product. From there, ASML is in the middle, while TSMC is the high-risk, high-reward pick. Overall, for investors with capital to put to work, these three businesses have the staying power to be solid investments over the next decade.

#3107. Microsoft blames major outage on a July update defect – and two other factors

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A surprise defect took more than 80% of Microsoft's servers out at the outage's peak. Here's what happened.

Microsoft has released new information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July update to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Low server capacity and peak traffic in the US brought the defect out of hiding, despite no prior reported issues.

“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable,” Lamanna said, noting that the update was deployed safely worldwide without any issues for over three months.

He said Microsoft didn’t find the issue in testing due to “the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” because “our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.”

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Two other factors made matters worse, and left servers useless in less than two hours.

“A surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention,” Lamanna said, explaining that Microsoft 365 maintains two gateway systems. Before the outage started, Teams failed from one to the other, which “changed its traffic patterns.” Simultaneously, he added, “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.”

Those two conditions collided and “caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna concluded. Requests eventually overloaded servers, at which point they stopped responding. At the outage’s low point, over 80% of its servers weren’t responding.

“When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route users to other healthy endpoints,” Lamanna said. “However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers.”

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

Before Microsoft issued an explanation, some suspected the outage may have been the result of a cyberattack, which both Lamanna and Microsoft’s status account denied.

It’s unclear how many people the outage affected, though Microsoft’s own numbers from January say Microsoft 365 “exceeds 450 million commercial paid seats,” illustrating the scale of the issue. Microsoft deployed an update to fix the outage and gradually applied it to groups of servers. Lamanna said Microsoft would publish a full post-incident review with more details later this week.

Service might be restored, but customers aren’t happy about having lost nearly two full workdays. One think tank told CNN it estimated the outage — which lasted through close of business on Friday for some — resulted in $7 billion in losses, due to many businesses and organizations being unable to access their everyday systems.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

The fact that Microsoft’s testing couldn’t find the July issue ahead of time may leave customers wondering when the next dormant defect will strike, and whether the company is prepared.

Organizations across Europe have been leaving Microsoft in recent years, opting instead for locally-controlled, open-source alternatives. The former CEO of Github launched a decentralized alternative called Entire earlier this year, citing developers’ need for something more reliable, as Github has similarly been plagued with outages.

For many, Teams was barely offline over the two-day period, or was the first service to come back online.

“Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without issue for most of the outage,” Lamanna explained. Other services like Exchange Online can’t fail out.

He added that fixing the outage was slow because waiting traffic hit servers as soon as they came back, rendering them unresponsive just as quickly.

“Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state,” Lamanna said. “Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”

On Thursday morning, people began reporting issues with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

As late as Friday afternoon, the company didn’t yet have an ETA of when the outage would be fully solved.

#3105. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3102. I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Review: Xiaomi's 18 Pro Max is a quirky Android phone that stands out from the crowd with its extra screen on the back. Shame Americans can't have it.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year. But it was sold only in China. Being from the UK, I went back to my regular boring phone with its boring single screen. Big sigh. So imagine my excitement when Xiaomi announced that its new flagship 18 Pro and Pro Max — complete with a second rear screen — would launch internationally, with a rollout including the UK and wider Europe. As with the rest of Xiaomi’s handsets, people in the US are flat out of luck.

That sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good. I worried that the rear screen would just be a dumb gimmick — something that tries to separate the phone from competitors but doesn’t actually add anything useful. But I actually like it. Need it? No. But it’s fun and has some genuine uses.

Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year.

The 18 Pro isn’t just smaller (6.4 inches vs. the Pro Max’s 6.9 inches) it misses some of the Max’s top tech as well. The processor is a lesser model, the main camera doesn’t use LOFIC tech and the smaller battery isn’t as capable. Shame.

But the 18 Pro Max is an all-round Android powerhouse, and I’ve really enjoyed getting to grips with it over the past couple of weeks. Here’s what I’ve found and what you need to know about this phone.

The extra display on the back is certainly this phone’s standout feature. It’s basically in the same place as the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera island, but instead of just being a piece of metal, it’s an actual functioning screen. If you’ve ever seen the cover display on a clamshell flip phone like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, then it’ll seem quite familiar.

Like the Flip 8, the second display shows incoming notifications, acting as a camera viewfinder and offering a variety of basic built-in functions like calendar reminders. What really hooked me, though, was the ability to create Gen AI apps just by typing in a prompt.

For example, I asked for “a game where you just pop bubbles,” which the “Polish” tool elaborated on with deeper functions and visual styles before generating a finished game that was fully playable on the back screen, complete with a scoring system and, for some reason, a jellyfish mascot. It takes about 5 minutes for the app to be created each time, and its functions are limited. It’s not able to access any app data, so don’t expect to create a new email reader, and anything too technical will result in failure.

I asked it to create a camera overlay that showed exposure settings (shutter speed, ISO and so on) to serve as a light meter for an analog camera. I’m not sure whether the issue was my explanation or a technical limitation, but it took the phone two tries to get something close. It created an interface with dials and exposure information, but it didn’t open the camera to calculate exposure as I’d hoped. As a result, it looked nice but it was functionally redundant.

Another time, I asked it to create an app that showed real-time charging speeds. The resulting app showed current battery level but not charging speed. It did have a baffling “charging milestones completed” button that simply increased by one each time I tapped it. I also had no luck with my “rude word generator,” which just repeatedly came back with “Couldn’t generate.” Frustratingly, each time it fails to create an app, it doesn’t tell you why — like if you’re asking for information it’s unable to access — but just says to try again “in a minute or two,” which rarely resulted in success in my testing time. If I’m asking for something it can’t achieve, it’d be helpful to know that.

Even so, I’m impressed with this app creation tool and, like many of the AI tools that only mildly excite me right now, I can only assume it will improve over time.

One of my favorite uses of the rear screen, though, is for vlogging. Firstly, seeing yourself from the back of the phone means you’re able to accurately film yourself using the best quality camera, rather than limiting yourself to the front-facing camera, which won’t look as good. But there’s also an autocue function where you can input a script and have it overlaid as text, allowing you to read out your words as you present to camera.

It’s a powerful tool for vloggers and other video creators who rely on longer prewritten scripts for their videos. But it’s quite basic: the text simply auto-scrolls at a speed you set in advance. I’d love to see Xiaomi use voice recognition here to automatically progress the text as you read out the words, slowing down or speeding up as you naturally read aloud. This tech already exists, so I don’t think I’m asking for literal magic here.

Tucked into that second display is a 200-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel telephoto camera offering 3.2x optical zoom or 6.4x hybrid zoom. There’s also a really tiny 50-megapixel ultrawide camera by itself below the camera island, which makes it feel like an afterthought — something that I’ll come back to later.

The main sensor is physically slightly smaller than the one in Xiaomi’s Leitzphone, but it uses the same LOFIC sensor tech for better dynamic range in a single image. I’ve taken a lot of photos with it so far and I’m really impressed with what I’ve seen. The smaller 18 Pro has an almost identical camera setup but its main sensor doesn’t use LOFIC, which is a shame as it forces you to go for the larger phone if you want the best possible image quality.

Shots are well-exposed, with accurate colors and fine details that manage to look sharp but without the harsh over-sharpened look that’s all too often seen from phone cameras. Images look more natural as a result.

There are a lot of ways to tune your images in-camera — almost too many, in fact. There’s a whole host of built-in color presets, including a Leica-branded high-contrast black-and-white mode that I like, all of which you can customize further by adjusting the tones, colors, grain and white balance. Then there’s the option to shoot using the phone’s default color processing, going with “Leica Vibrant” for more popping colors or “Leica Authentic” for more natural tones. Each of these applies no matter what filter you then apply over the top.

Confused? Yeah, I’m not entirely surprised, there are a lot of variables at play when taking an image with this thing but it didn’t take me long to figure out how to get the look that I wanted. And let’s be honest, there aren’t many photographers who want fewer options in how to take a photo.

Then there’s Essential Moment, which is its own standalone mode where you can select from three distinct styles: a black and white mode, “modern vintage,” or “Iconic CCD.” Each of these is designed to replicate specific looks from cameras of the past, and Xiaomi says it uses AI to analyze the scene to authentically reproduce color tones, vintage lens effects and film grain (though crucially not generative AI to actually alter anything in the scene).

I actually love this, especially the black and white option, which produces monochrome images with beautiful contrast and genuinely authentic-looking film grain. It’s the mode I’d end up using most often, I’m sure, and I’ve taken a bunch of photos with it that I really like.

Oh, and that tiny ultrawide camera, weirdly separated from its friends? It’s not great, with nighttime shots being particularly disappointing here. On the upside, the main camera’s standard focal length is 23mm, which is already pretty wide, so you probably won’t miss the ultrawide much.

While the base 18 Pro uses Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the Pro Max ups the ante with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. It’s no surprise that the Pro Max is a seriously powerful bit of kit, returning benchmark scores up there with the powerhouse Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Everything ran exceptionally smoothly, from playing demanding 3D games like Genshin Impact to editing photos or navigating the Android 17 interface. I found much the same with the 18 Pro, too — I didn’t see a noticeable difference in performance.

I don’t mind Xiaomi’s software skin, as it’s easy enough for anyone familiar with Android to get to grips with. What I don’t like, though, is the company’s insistence on preloading it with an armada of apps including AliExpress, Netflix, WPS Office, TikTok and others. Together with the variety of Xiaomi apps also on board, the phone feels somewhat cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to add anything of your own. I’ve seen worse examples (Oppo has been bad with this), but it still irks me that the phone ends up feeling almost like it’s ad-supported. And if it is, surely it should be cheaper?

It helps a bit, sure, but it won’t block those creeps entirely. My advice is: if you’ve got information so sensitive that even a glimpse would be career-ending, maybe wait until you’re alone before you put it on screen.

The 7,050-mAh silicon-carbon battery in the larger Pro Max packs a punch, putting in some solid scores on our demanding battery rundown tests. After one hour of YouTube streaming, it dropped to 97%, then to 89% after the third hour. That puts it above the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, although still below the current champion, the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

In everyday use, you won’t struggle to get through a full day of mixed use and you can likely be quite demanding with it and still not worry about it conking out mid-afternoon. Take photos, watch videos, listen to music – don’t stress over it; this thing should hold out fine.

The phone supports up to 100-watt wired fast charging, though you’ll need a Xiaomi fast charger to achieve the fastest speeds. I don’t have a Xiaomi charger (and the fastest it sells in the UK is 90W for £25), but I tried it with multiple third-party 100-watt chargers and the maximum I could get was around 65 watts. Even so, it went from 1% to 65% in 30 minutes of charging, which is still pretty quick — on par with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, in fact. Still, it should be able to go faster; you’ll just need to source a charger that will allow it.

With its smaller 6,000-mAh battery the Xiaomi 18 Pro didn’t fare as well on our battery drain tests (it dropped to 93% after an hour of YouTube streaming) but in general use you’ll still comfortably get through most of a day on a single charge.

If you’re in the US, it’s something of a moot point. You can’t buy it. Sorry. Sure, you can probably import it from some third-party resellers, but it’s not officially on sale.

If you’re somewhere where you can buy it, then lucky you — this phone is a blast. It ticks many of the boxes I’d expect from a flagship phone right now (camera quality in particular), and that second rear screen is the cherry on top. I expected it to feel like a pointless gimmick, and maybe it is a bit of a novelty, but it’s fun and I’ve already found it genuinely useful.

I don’t like that there are so many hardware differences between the two phone sizes, as it forces you to have a much bigger model if you want the best performance. I prefer Apple’s approach: With the iPhone 18 Pro, I can have the same exact potent camera setup and processor performance, no matter which size I choose. With Xiaomi’s phones I’m forced to compromise between performance and pocketability. If you want the best camera, then go for the bigger model. Battery life is better, too.

#3101. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

Samsung’s Galaxy AI may be getting a cross-app intelligence upgrade, à la Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Siri AI, according to an Android Authority report. Samsung is working on Galaxy Claw, which could make Galaxy AI more agentic and context-aware across your apps.

Also: Samsung mulls Galaxy AI usage limits and subscription tiers

Currently, Galaxy AI lives inside your Galaxy devices and apps, but its smarts are limited to the apps it’s integrated with. Android Authority reports that Samsung’s Personal Agent Core is at the center of Galaxy Claw, connecting Galaxy AI to compatible apps and services, such as Calendar, Contacts, Messages, Gmail, Gallery, Phone, and Voice Recorder.

Android Authority found code that referred to Galaxy Claw in Samsung’s Personal Agent Core app, suggesting that Galaxy AI can complete cross-app tasks. For example, take the request: “Remind me to buy Mom a birthday card two days before her birthday.” An assistant without access to multiple apps will set a reminder to buy Mom a birthday card, but you might have to manually enter the date and time for the reminder to notify you.

With a more agentic assistant, it can access Mom’s contact card and her birthdate, calculate two days before her birthday, and remind you on that date. Like Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI, Personal Agent Core will need special permissions to access your sensitive information, such as messages, photos, and calls.

Gmail features a Gemini-powered daily brief, which compiles information from my email inbox and GChat messages to show me things I may have missed. I find it very useful for work, since my inbox is flooded and I often miss important emails.

Also: I’m a ChatGPT power user, but I won’t give it my wallet

#3095. iPhone Duo 2 prototypes suggest Face ID, Action Button, other potential 2027 features

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With manufacturing deadlines looming, it's unclear which of several feature upgrades may have to wait until the foldable's third generation.

Although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its plans for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down

iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its new smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

The report indicates that many users don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

Apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give users greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

Technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower

For many users, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

Because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

#3094. I’ve Used VSCO’s Lightroom Rival Desktop Editor and It’s Great for Creatives

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

VSCO might be popular for iPhone photography, but its Studio Pro has rival Adobe firmly in its sights.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

VSCO is best known these days for its iPhone and Android editing app that makes pics look all cool and analog. But the company is launching its first stand-alone desktop photo editor for Mac, called VSCO Studio Pro, bringing its famous filmic presets—and a wealth of editing tools. I’ve used it, and while it’s not yet my sole image-editing solution, it’s great for getting those dreamy vintage vibes out of your photos.

The desktop app will be immediately familiar to any photographer who’s spent any time in Lightroom or Capture One. There are exposure, contrast, highlight, and shadow sliders along with color sliders for white balance or individual color adjustments. It’s par for the course for any raw image editor.

VSCO’s wide range of color presets has always been where it shines the brightest. Numbering just north of 200, Studio Pro packs in all the presets, from color classics like the company’s A1-10 range to a wealth of black-and-white options and a host of presets designed to emulate real film stocks like Kodak Gold or Fuji Velvia. VSCO says these are modeled on real scans of these film stocks to make them as authentic as possible.

It’s the presets that I love the most in VSCO’s app. Years ago, the company sold its presets as a downloadable Lightroom preset pack, which I have used in my photography workflow almost daily for the past 13 years, and their look is identical here. While it hasn’t sold the Lightroom preset pack in about a decade, VSCO’s Studio Pro app finally lets photographers achieve those same looks in desktop editing.

With Studio Pro, VSCO clearly has its sights on Lightroom. While Adobe is increasingly filling its services with various generative AI tools that radically alter your image’s content, VSCO is taking a more stripped-back approach that focuses on the creative side of color and exposure adjustments.

It’s still quite bare-bones at launch, with several features I need for my own photography missing, like masking. I can’t make selective edits to my images—like using a gradient to tone down the highlights only in the sky. Apparently this is coming soon, as are bloom and halation tools, which are already in the app, but grayed out with a “soon” marker next to them. Ditto the spot removal tool for cleaning up dust or sensor spots.

The big thing for me, though, comes down to cataloging and archiving of my images. I have several terabytes of images cataloged in my Lightroom library, available to edit on any device I sign in on — including phone, tablet or desktop. While VSCO will have some basic organization options within the Studio Pro app (grouping images into “Projects”—again, coming soon), it’s not as full-featured as Lightroom’s archiving system. I worry that once I’m working with thousands of images across multiple photoshoots, things will quickly become cluttered and difficult to navigate. Time will tell.

I don’t imagine VSCO’s app will necessarily be the first choice for working pros who need strict cataloging, backups and remote access. I count myself in that category, and for me Lightroom’s cloud storage remains the biggest reason to stay with Adobe, while others swear by Capture One for its Sessions-based filing system and its tethered shooting workflow.

By contrast, I see VSCO Studio Pro appealing more to enthusiast photographers who want to efficiently add real creative flair to their images and don’t necessarily want to spend on the commercial tools, cloud storage, or AI options offered by Adobe.

#3093. The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

#3092. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security leaders reveal the future consequences of AI outpacing human defenders.

At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s new security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

However, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security issues introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

I love a hack, especially when it comes to training legs. If you don't want to lift heavy weights but you do want to improve lower-body strength and mobility, let me introduce you to one exercise that will change the game for you.

Check out the exercise below, how to do it, and the benefits for your body.

The Cossack Squat is an underrated bodyweight exercise. Unlike standard squats or lunges, you load one leg at a time with a deep lateral (side-to-side) plane of motion, which builds single-leg strength, adductor flexibility and resilience and joint mobility.

Here's a step-by-step guide on how to do them:

This move hits a lot of muscles, including your core for trunk stabilization, and your hip flexors, quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves and lower back.

What I love most is that unilateral loading creates plenty of tension in the working muscles to achieve overload without weights. At the same time, you build frontal-plane strength by moving side-to-side, which is important for targeting muscles like the adductors and outer hips. Strengthening as many muscles as you can means your body will be more resilient during rotation or big, heavy lifts.

Applied Materials stock is too cheap to ignore given the incredible growth it has been clocking.

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 18, 2026 at 6:36AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Applied Materials ›

The semiconductor sector has witnessed turbulence in the second half of 2026, as evidenced by a 28% drop in the PHLX Semiconductor Sector since the beginning of July.

The pullback has been triggered by various factors, including a September rate hike by the Federal Reserve, the possibility of further hikes to keep inflation under control, and the viability of robust artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending amid a high-interest rate environment. These headwinds have crushed some top semiconductor stocks lately, including Applied Materials (AMAT +1.36%).

Shares of Applied Materials have retreated 46% since the beginning of July. However, a closer look at the company's latest quarterly results clearly suggests that the stock's sell-off is overdone. Let's look at the reasons why Applied Materials stock is a top buy right now.

Applied Materials released fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results (for the year ended Oct. 25) on Nov. 12. The company's revenue jumped by an impressive 53% from the year-ago period to a record $10.41 billion. In fact, its quarterly revenue growth was significantly higher than the annual revenue increase of 21% to $34.45 billion.

Even better, Applied Materials' non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) increased by 92% year over year to $4.16 in the previous quarter. That was well above the company's fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS growth of 37% to $12.89.

It is quite easy to see why Applied Materials' growth accelerated remarkably in the previous quarter. The company sells wafer and fabrication (WFE) equipment that's used by semiconductor foundries, integrated device manufacturers (IDMs), and memory manufacturers to make chips. The strong demand from the foundry/logic and memory markets for advanced AI chips has been a massive tailwind for Applied Materials.

Importantly, Applied Materials expects the momentum to continue in 2027, predicting a 30% increase in WFE demand next year. What's more, the company is confident it can grow faster than the WFE market by gaining more share in this space. Industry association SEMI predicts that the WFE market could clock 23% growth in 2026, and Applied Materials' growth last quarter clearly suggests that it is growing significantly faster than the broader market.

SEMI expects a 21% increase in WFE sales next year. However, Applied Materials is more confident in this market's growth due to the construction of new semiconductor fabs worldwide. Management noted on the latest earnings call that the "demand for advanced semiconductors remains much higher than supply, and multi-year investments [in] new fab capacity are needed for the industry to close this supply-demand gap."

Consulting firm McKinsey also recently raised its 2030 global semiconductor industry revenue forecast to $2.3 trillion, up from $1.6 trillion, noting that demand for advanced chips to support the AI build-out will be a tailwind for the sector. So, Applied Materials' impressive growth momentum isn't going away any time soon.

This explains why the company's guidance for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 points to an improvement in its financial performance. Applied Materials expects $11.1 billion in revenue this quarter, implying a 58% increase over the prior-year period. The non-GAAP EPS forecast of $4.35 points to an 83% increase over last year.

What's worth noting is that Applied Materials' revenue fell slightly in the same quarter last year, while its EPS was flat on a year-over-year basis. So, healthy investments in AI data center infrastructure are now driving stronger growth, and that trend seems sustainable given the semiconductor industry's long-term growth potential.

Each share of Applied Materials trades at just under $400, as of this writing. So, if you've $500 in investable cash right now after meeting your expenses, saving for difficult times, and clearing high-interest debt, you can consider putting that money into Applied Materials stock.

That's because the company is not just clocking terrific growth; its recent slide has made it extremely attractive from a valuation perspective. Applied Materials trades at just 21 times forward earnings, a discount to the iShares Semiconductor ETF's price-to-earnings ratio of 39. That's quite attractive for a company whose EPS is poised to grow at a healthy rate over the next three years.

Apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in the press release.

Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this new health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

If you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.
